_README: Per-question INTERNAL escalation guide for the live examiner. Keyed by question number (matching oral_exam_questions_list.txt and molecule_map.json). 'probes' are progressively deeper escalation TARGETS (concepts to push toward, not phrasings to read out); 'misconception' is the common wrong idea to watch for and probe. This content is injected into the examiner prompt as non-disclosed guidance and must never be shown to the student. Questions absent from this file simply get no extra guidance. Covers all topics (Q1-100; Q16 is intentionally absent from the bank). Entries match the current question wording, including re-angled questions (19, 28, 40, 50, 52, 55, 76, 80) and de-named stems.

1.misconception: Thinking a small reagent shortfall has only a negligible or non-linear effect, or reasoning from mass shortfall without converting to moles via the balanced ratio.
probes: Quantify the proportionality: if the loaded NaN3 is ~10% short, what happens to the moles (and therefore volume) of N2 produced?
Write and balance the decomposition (2 NaN3 -> 2 Na + 3 N2) and use the mole ratio to relate moles of azide to moles of N2.
Connect moles of N2 to the inflated volume via the ideal gas law (V proportional to n at fixed T and P).
Surface the assumptions behind the strict proportionality: reaction goes to completion, fixed T and P.

2.misconception: Believing the assay measures protein directly, or that any nitrogen-containing additive inflates the reading equally regardless of its mass-percent nitrogen.
probes: Why is nitrogen used as a proxy for protein at all (a fixed nitrogen-to-protein conversion factor)?
Why is melamine's mass-percent nitrogen so high - reason from its formula (C3H6N6) and molar mass.
Estimate the effect: with a ~6.25 conversion factor, roughly how much apparent 'protein' does a gram of melamine fake?
What measurement would distinguish genuine protein nitrogen from melamine nitrogen?

3.misconception: Thinking a percent yield below 100% means atoms were destroyed, or conflating percent yield with purity or percent composition.
probes: Define percent yield (actual / theoretical x 100) and state what the 'theoretical' value assumes.
Distinguish the possible causes: incomplete reaction, competing side reactions, and physical losses - which lower the yield?
Reconcile with conservation of mass: if only 78% of the ethanol formed, where did the rest of the carbon go?
How could the brewer push the yield higher (drive the reaction further, suppress side products)?

4.misconception: Confusing amount of substance (moles) with concentration; assuming a correctly sized tablet gives the right concentration regardless of water volume.
probes: Why does the same tablet give a different ppm in pools of different size (c = n / V)?
Carry out the calculation: given the moles of HOCl released and the pool volume, find the concentration.
What happens to the free-chlorine concentration as water evaporates or is topped up (dilution)?
Separate the two quantities: which does the tablet fix (amount), and which does the pool set (volume), and how do they combine?

5.misconception: Identifying the leftover reactant as the limiting one, or assuming more charcoal is always better without considering excess-carbon contamination.
probes: When carbon is short, which species is limiting and which is left over?
Write the reduction (e.g. 2 Fe2O3 + 3 C -> 4 Fe + 3 CO2) and use the mole ratio.
Describe the product when carbon is limiting (unreduced oxide / slag) versus when carbon is in excess (carbon mixed into the iron).
How does the limiting reagent set the maximum mass of iron obtainable from a given charge?

6.misconception: Assuming that because both reagents are physically present the reaction must run fully; overlooking that an unreleased reagent does not participate.
probes: Why does releasing only part of the H2O2 make it the limiting reagent even though 'both reagents are present'?
Relate the moles of excited intermediate (and hence photons emitted) to the moles of limiting H2O2.
Would fully cracking the ampoule restore full brightness - and what else could still limit it?
Distinguish brightness (amount/rate of light) from how long the glow lasts.

7.misconception: Treating excess reagent as wasteful or as an error, and confusing the logic of a back-titration with a direct titration.
probes: Why must the analyte (ethanol) be completely consumed in a back-titration?
What is actually measured (the leftover dichromate), and how does that yield the ethanol amount by difference?
What goes wrong if dichromate is limiting (unreacted ethanol -> the alcohol content is underestimated)?
Use the redox stoichiometry (ethanol oxidized, Cr(VI) -> Cr(III)) to back-calculate the ethanol consumed.

8.misconception: Treating the carbon anode as an inert electrode/spectator rather than a consumed reactant tied stoichiometrically to the product.
probes: Why does consumption of the carbon anode stoichiometrically limit how much aluminum can be deposited?
Write the cell reaction (2 Al2O3 + 3 C -> 4 Al + 3 CO2) and state the C-to-Al mole ratio.
For a strong student: connect charge passed (Faraday's laws) to the moles of aluminum deposited.
Why must the anodes be replenished periodically for production to continue?

9.misconception: Confusing per-pass conversion with overall yield, or believing the unreacted feed is destroyed/lost rather than recoverable.
probes: Why does a 70% per-pass conversion leave 30% of the feed unreacted (not consumed)?
How does recycling the unreacted heptane raise the overall yield toward 100% over multiple passes?
Clearly distinguish per-pass conversion from cumulative overall yield.
Why is recycling preferred to discarding (feedstock cost, atom economy)?

10.misconception: Thinking the reaction keeps going as long as any reagent remains, and not linking the limiting reagent to the measurable signal (color change).
probes: Why is ethanol the limiting reagent here (small breath sample against a fixed amount of dichromate)?
Why does the color change stop once the ethanol is gone, even though dichromate remains?
Why is the degree of color change proportional to the ethanol present - the basis for quantifying it?
Identify which species is oxidized and which reduced, and why Cr(VI) -> Cr(III) produces the color change.

11.misconception: Believing pressure can only rise from a chemical reaction or by 'creating' molecules, rather than from a phase change adding gas-phase molecules.
probes: Where do the gas molecules come from if no reaction occurs (a solid-to-gas phase change)?
Relate the added moles of gas to pressure at fixed volume and temperature (PV = nRT).
What happens to the pressure as more dry ice sublimes, and what finally limits it (vessel strength / equilibrium)?
Contrast with a true chemical reaction: is the total number of molecules conserved here?

12.misconception: Assuming all gases behave ideally, or that molar mass alone (not intermolecular forces) governs deviation from ideal behavior.
probes: What molecular property makes a real gas deviate from ideal behavior (intermolecular attractions)?
Compare CO and water: why does water's hydrogen bonding cause larger deviation than CO's weak forces?
Under what conditions (low temperature, high pressure) do these deviations become most pronounced?
For a strong student: which van der Waals term (a, attractions) captures this difference?

13.misconception: Believing the pressure dropped because air leaked out, rather than recognizing the temperature dependence of pressure at fixed n and V.
probes: With no air escaping, which variable changed to lower the pressure (temperature)?
State the relationship between P and absolute temperature at constant V and n.
Why must temperature be in kelvin for this proportionality to hold?
Estimate roughly how much the pressure drops for a given temperature change (proportional reasoning).

14.misconception: Thinking the bubbles are newly created gas, rather than dissolved gas leaving solution as its solubility falls with pressure.
probes: Why does opening the cap cause CO2 to leave solution (the pressure above the liquid drops)?
Relate gas solubility to the partial pressure above the liquid (Henry's law).
Where was the CO2 before opening - why were no 'new' molecules created?
Why does warm soda go flat faster (temperature dependence of gas solubility)?

15.misconception: Treating boiling point as a fixed property of a liquid, independent of the surrounding pressure.
probes: What condition defines boiling in terms of vapor pressure and external pressure?
Why does lowering the external pressure lower the boiling temperature?
How does this let distillers separate heat-sensitive compounds at gentler temperatures?
Connect to altitude: why does water boil below 100 C on a mountain?

17.misconception: Attributing the temperature rise to the gas being 'squeezed into less space' rather than to work done on the molecules raising their kinetic energy.
probes: What is happening to the molecules' speeds / kinetic energy as the piston does work on them?
Link average molecular kinetic energy to temperature.
Why must the compression be rapid (adiabatic) for the temperature to rise noticeably?
Contrast slow compression with heat allowed to escape - why is the result different?

18.misconception: Asserting 'more heat means more pressure' without connecting temperature to molecular speed and collision frequency/force.
probes: What happens to molecular speeds as temperature rises (the kinetic-energy/temperature relationship)?
How do faster molecules change the frequency and force of wall collisions?
Tie collision frequency and force back to the macroscopic pressure on the casing.
At fixed volume, what does this predict for the pressure-temperature relationship?

19.misconception: Assuming real gases always exert higher pressure than ideal, or attributing all deviation to molecular volume regardless of conditions.
probes: What intermolecular feature reduces the force of wall collisions below the ideal prediction (attractions)?
Identify which van der Waals correction this is (the -a(n/V)^2 term).
Why do attractions dominate at moderate pressure but the finite molecular volume (b term) dominate at very high pressure?
For a strong student: describe how the compressibility factor Z sits below or above 1 in each regime.

20.misconception: Thinking only molar mass matters, or that larger molecules are somehow 'more ideal'.
probes: Why do larger, more polarizable molecules experience stronger London dispersion forces?
How does the finite molecular volume of a large molecule violate an ideal-gas assumption?
Why does butane, being smaller and less polarizable, track ideal behavior more closely?
Which ideal-gas assumptions (no attractions, negligible volume) are most strained by tetraethyllead?

21.misconception: Confusing the visible fizz with the equilibrium shift, or not identifying the stress (lower headspace CO2 pressure) that drives it.
probes: Identify the equilibrium (dissolved CO2 <-> gaseous CO2) and the stress applied on opening.
Which direction does lowering the headspace CO2 pressure drive the system, and why?
Is the Le Chatelier description and a Henry's-law description capturing the same shift?
Why does the burst eventually stop (a new equilibrium / depleted dissolved CO2)?

22.misconception: Thinking added acid directly 'attacks' CaCO3, rather than removing carbonate product and pulling the dissolution equilibrium forward.
probes: Write the relevant equilibria (CaCO3 dissolution; H+ + CO3^2- -> HCO3-).
How does consuming carbonate ion shift the dissolution equilibrium (Le Chatelier)?
Why does that make calcium carbonate skeletons dissolve more readily?
Connect to acidification: why does rising dissolved CO2 lower carbonate availability?

23.misconception: Treating fermentation as freely reversible, or not connecting rising product partial pressure to Q exceeding K.
probes: Identify the gaseous product whose buildup applies the stress.
How does increasing a product's partial pressure change the reaction quotient Q relative to K?
Which direction does the system shift to restore equilibrium, slowing the net forward process?
For a strong student: why is venting CO2 used in practice to keep fermentation going?

24.misconception: Confusing which form is favored by lower pH, or not seeing added H+ as the stress on the dissociation equilibrium.
probes: Write HOCl <-> H+ + OCl- and identify the stress when pH is lowered (more H+).
Which direction does added H+ drive the equilibrium, and which species is favored?
Why does that increase the fraction present as the neutral HOCl?
Connect to disinfection: why is HOCl the more effective germicide than OCl-?

25.misconception: Thinking the instrument must measure blood directly, or that the breath/blood ratio is arbitrary rather than a fixed partition at body temperature.
probes: Why does a fixed equilibrium ratio let a breath measurement stand in for the blood concentration?
What does the ~2100:1 partition coefficient represent physically?
Why does body temperature need to be roughly constant for this to hold?
What would happen to the estimate if the actual ratio differed from the assumed one?

26.misconception: Memorizing 'higher temperature shifts right' without recognizing that this depends on the reaction being endothermic (heat as a reactant).
probes: For an endothermic reaction, where does 'heat' effectively sit (the reactant side)?
Why does adding heat (raising T) shift the equilibrium toward products here?
How would the answer differ if the reaction were exothermic?
For a strong student: how does raising T change the value of K itself, not just the position?

27.misconception: Assuming hotter water dissolves more of every solute, rather than tying it to the endothermic enthalpy of dissolution.
probes: For an endothermic dissolution, how does heat behave (like a reactant)?
Why does raising temperature increase the equilibrium amount dissolved?
Give a counterexample - a gas whose solubility decreases with temperature - and explain the difference.
Distinguish the rate of dissolving from the equilibrium amount dissolved.

28.misconception: Reading the color change as an irreversible reaction or simple kinetics, rather than a genuine, reversible equilibrium that temperature shifts.
probes: Why is this a true reversible equilibrium rather than a one-way reaction (the color returns)?
How does temperature behave like a reactant or product when the reaction has a nonzero enthalpy?
Predict the color-change direction on heating if the forward reaction is endothermic.
Why can restoring the original temperature restore the original color, unlike a decomposition?

29.misconception: Thinking the amount of solid affects the equilibrium position, or that solids are omitted from the expression arbitrarily.
probes: Why is the activity (effective concentration) of a pure solid constant regardless of amount?
How does that constancy let it be folded into K rather than written as a variable?
Predict: does adding more dry ice change the equilibrium gas pressure? Why or why not?
Does the same reasoning apply to a pure liquid?

30.misconception: Assuming Kp and Kc are always equal, or not connecting their difference to a change in the moles of gas.
probes: On what quantities are Kp and Kc each based (partial pressures vs molar concentrations)?
State the relationship Kp = Kc(RT)^(delta n) and define delta n.
For NO2/N2O4, work out delta n and explain why the constants differ numerically.
When would Kp and Kc be numerically equal (delta n = 0)?

31.misconception: Assuming an exothermic reaction's energy must go entirely into one channel (all light or all heat).
probes: Into what forms does the released chemical energy partition (photons versus heat)?
Why does an exothermic reaction guarantee that some energy warms the surroundings?
What would 'efficiency' of the chemiluminescent reaction mean in this framing?
Connect to enthalpy: is the warmth consistent with an overall negative delta H?

32.misconception: Describing it as merely 'getting hot' without the positive-feedback link between heat released and reaction rate.
probes: Why does heat released by one decomposition speed up neighboring decompositions (Arrhenius)?
How does that create a self-reinforcing (positive-feedback) loop?
What is the specific role of the exothermicity (versus an endothermic process)?
What could interrupt the loop (cooling faster than heat is generated)?

33.misconception: Assuming an external heat source is needed, or ignoring the role of pile size/insulation in heat accumulation.
probes: What reaction releases the heat (exothermic microbial oxidation of organic matter)?
Why does a large, insulated pile get hot while a thin layer does not (generation versus dissipation)?
Trace the energy bookkeeping - where does the chemical energy go?
Why might the pile eventually stop heating (substrate depletion, drying out)?

34.misconception: Believing more reaction steps means a different total enthalpy, i.e. treating enthalpy as path-dependent.
probes: What property of enthalpy makes the total change depend only on initial and final states?
Why does the number of intermediate steps not affect the overall delta H?
How would you sum the step enthalpies to get the overall value?
Would the same path-independence hold for the reaction rate? Why not?

35.misconception: Thinking a complex multi-step browning has a path-dependent energy, or conflating enthalpy with rate/mechanism.
probes: Why is the total delta H independent of the intermediate cascade (state function)?
How could you use known step enthalpies to find the overall change?
Distinguish what depends on path (rate, mechanism) from what does not (delta H).
Why is this principle useful when intermediates are hard to measure directly?

36.misconception: Thinking bond breaking releases energy (it costs energy), or reversing the broken/formed bookkeeping.
probes: Does breaking a bond absorb or release energy? And forming one?
Set up the estimate: sum(bonds broken) minus sum(bonds formed).
What does a positive versus negative result tell you (endothermic versus exothermic)?
Why is this only an estimate (average bond enthalpies versus actual values)?

37.misconception: Attributing the cracks to the chemistry alone rather than to differential thermal expansion from uneven heat dissipation.
probes: Why does the interior stay hotter than the surface during curing (heat dissipation)?
How does differential expansion and contraction create tensile stress?
Why does exceeding the tensile strength cause cracking?
What mitigation follows from this (slow curing, cooling pipes)?

38.misconception: Not connecting a measured temperature rise to heat via q = mcDeltaT, or forgetting to normalize per mole.
probes: What equation converts the water's temperature rise into the heat absorbed (q = mcDeltaT)?
Under what assumption does that heat equal the reaction's enthalpy release (no heat loss)?
How do you convert total heat into delta H per mole (divide by moles of H2O2)?
What experimental errors would bias the result (heat loss, incomplete reaction)?

39.misconception: Concluding that because no warmth is felt, the reaction is not exothermic - conflating thermodynamics with rate.
probes: Separate the two questions: is rusting exothermic (thermodynamics) versus how fast (kinetics)?
Why does a very slow reaction release its heat too slowly to feel?
What controls the rate here (activation energy, ambient conditions)?
Contrast with a fast exothermic reaction (combustion) that clearly feels hot.

40.misconception: Confusing heat capacity with temperature, or assuming all materials change temperature equally for the same heat input.
probes: Why does water's high specific heat mean only a small temperature change for a given heat (q = mcDeltaT)?
Why do rock and sand, with lower heat capacities, swing more in temperature?
How does the ocean exchanging heat with the air buffer coastal temperatures?
Distinguish heat (energy) from temperature in this scenario.

41.misconception: Believing a negative delta G guarantees an observable rate.
probes: What does delta G tell you (direction/favorability) versus what it does not (rate)?
Why does a large activation barrier make a favorable transformation imperceptibly slow?
What is 'kinetic stability' (metastability)?
What conditions could actually speed the diamond-to-graphite conversion (very high temperature)?

42.misconception: Predicting the wrong sign of the entropy change, or ignoring that producing many (especially gaseous) molecules raises disorder.
probes: What happens to the number of accessible microstates when one large molecule becomes many small ones?
Why does producing gases (CO2, water vapor) strongly increase entropy?
Predict the sign of delta S and justify it.
How does this entropy term factor into spontaneity (the TDeltaS term in delta G)?

43.misconception: Thinking the energy invested to make a molecule protects it thermodynamically (treating spontaneity as history-dependent).
probes: Does spontaneity depend on how a molecule was made, or only on current versus product free energy?
Why are the hydrolysis products lower in free energy than intact mRNA?
Reconcile: how can something expensive to synthesize still degrade spontaneously?
What then keeps mRNA intact in practice (kinetics / storage conditions)?

44.misconception: Assuming endothermic processes cannot be spontaneous, ignoring the entropy term.
probes: Write delta G = delta H - TDeltaS and identify the signs for sublimation.
Why does the large positive delta S (solid to gas) drive spontaneity?
Why is there a threshold temperature (-78 C) for spontaneity?
Below that temperature, which term wins and what happens?

45.misconception: Assuming entropy always favors spontaneity, or that both delta H and delta S must be favorable for delta G to be negative.
probes: What is the sign of the system's entropy change when O2 gas is consumed into a solid? Why?
Given the unfavorable entropy, which term must drive spontaneity (the exothermic delta H)?
Write delta G = delta H - TDeltaS and show how a negative delta H can dominate.
What would happen at very high temperature, where the TDeltaS term grows?

46.misconception: Treating spontaneity as fixed rather than temperature-dependent when delta H and delta S share the same sign.
probes: Given delta H > 0 and delta S > 0, how does raising T change delta G?
What defines the crossover temperature where delta G changes sign?
Why is the reaction non-spontaneous below it and spontaneous above?
Express that crossover temperature qualitatively in terms of delta H and delta S.

47.misconception: Confusing a faster rate at higher temperature with a more favorable delta G - conflating kinetics and thermodynamics.
probes: Why does delta G barely change while the rate changes a lot with temperature?
What controls the rate (the activation energy and the fraction of molecules above it)?
Distinguish 'how favorable' from 'how fast'.
Why does refrigeration slow degradation even when delta G is already negative?

48.misconception: Attributing persistence to thermodynamic stability when oxidation is actually favorable - the barrier is kinetic.
probes: Is complete oxidation of polyethylene thermodynamically favorable? What does that imply?
If favorable, why does it persist for centuries (a kinetic barrier)?
What makes the C-C and C-H bonds kinetically hard to break without enzymes or extreme conditions?
State the difference between thermodynamic stability and kinetic stability explicitly.

49.misconception: Thinking separation can be spontaneous, or ignoring that unmixing decreases entropy.
probes: What happens to entropy when a well-mixed system is separated into pure components?
Why, with no compensating exothermic enthalpy, does that make delta G positive?
How does the second law require external work for a non-spontaneous separation?
Why is isotope separation especially hard (the isotopes are chemically near-identical)?

50.misconception: Thinking energy conservation alone permits the reverse process, ignoring that total entropy must increase.
probes: Why does energy conservation alone not forbid the coffee reheating itself?
What additional law selects the allowed direction (the entropy of the universe must increase)?
Why does spreading thermal energy into the room increase the total number of microstates / entropy?
Connect to delta S_universe = delta S_system + delta S_surroundings > 0 for a spontaneous process.

51.misconception: Assuming more protons and electrons always means a larger ion, ignoring effective nuclear charge and shielding.
probes: Why are Cr3+ and Al3+ similar in size despite chromium having more protons and electrons?
How do poor shielding by 3d electrons and high nuclear charge contract the ion?
Why does similar size (and the same +3 charge) allow substitution into the lattice?
What would happen if the substituting ion were much larger or differently charged?

52.misconception: Treating metallic versus nonmetallic character as arbitrary rather than tracking it to periodic trends in ionization energy and electronegativity.
probes: How do effective nuclear charge, ionization energy, and electronegativity change across a period?
Why do left-side elements lose electrons easily (metallic) while right-side ones hold them (nonmetallic)?
Why does silicon's intermediate position give it intermediate (metalloid) behavior?
Predict how character changes down a group, and why.

53.misconception: Thinking covalent bonds have no ionic character, or that polarity does not affect bond strength.
probes: Why does fluorine's high electronegativity make the C-F bond very polar?
How does partial ionic character add to bond strength on top of covalent sharing?
Why does this make C-F unusually short and strong?
Connect to 'forever chemicals': why does a strong bond imply environmental persistence (kinetic)?

54.misconception: Assuming only chemical similarity matters, ignoring the role of matching ionic radius and charge for substitution.
probes: Why does a similar ionic radius and identical +2 charge let Pb2+ occupy Ca2+ sites?
How does fitting the coordination geometry of hydroxyapatite enable substitution?
What are the limits - how different could the radius be before substitution fails?
Why is this biologically dangerous (lead accumulating in bone)?

55.misconception: Expecting ionization energies to rise smoothly, not recognizing the large jump when removal breaks into a noble-gas core.
probes: Why is removing sodium's single 3s electron easy but the second electron very hard (it is a core electron)?
Why are magnesium's first and second ionization energies comparable (both valence 3s)?
Where does magnesium's large jump occur instead (the third ionization)?
How do successive-ionization-energy jumps reveal an element's group / valence-electron count?

56.misconception: Assuming isoelectronic species are the same size, ignoring differing nuclear charge.
probes: Why do Na+ and Mg2+ have the same number of electrons but different sizes?
How does Mg2+'s greater nuclear charge (12 versus 11 protons) contract its electron cloud?
State the general trend for radius across an isoelectronic series.
Predict the size order for an isoelectronic series (e.g. O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+).

57.misconception: Assuming silicon and carbon behave identically, or misjudging the direction/size of the electronegativity difference.
probes: How do the electronegativities of Si, C, and O compare?
Why is the Si-O bond more polar (more ionic character) than the C-O bond?
How does greater bond polarity affect bond length, strength, and flexibility?
Connect to the polymer backbone: why does this help oxygen permeability and flexibility?

58.misconception: Calling any interaction with hydrogen a 'hydrogen bond', or not tying N-H polarity to the electronegativity difference.
probes: Why is the N-H bond polar (electronegativity difference), and which atom carries the partial positive charge?
What does the partial-positive hydrogen need nearby to form a hydrogen bond (a lone pair on N/O/F)?
Distinguish the hydrogen bond from the covalent N-H bond itself.
Why does this matter for peptide structure and drug binding?

59.misconception: Attributing allotrope diversity to something other than carbon's small size and four valence electrons / hybridization flexibility.
probes: How do four valence electrons enable four covalent bonds in different hybridizations (sp, sp2, sp3)?
Why does carbon's small radius make those bonds short and strong?
How do different hybridizations lead to diamond versus graphite versus nanotubes?
Why can't most other elements form a comparable range of network structures?

60.misconception: Thinking neutron number (mass) affects chemical bonding, rather than electron configuration.
probes: What determines chemical bonding - proton/electron count or neutron count?
Why do C-12 and C-14 share identical electron configurations and reactivity?
What properties DO differ between isotopes (mass, nuclear stability)?
For a strong student: why can mass cause small kinetic-isotope rate effects while leaving the chemistry the same?

61.misconception: Assuming a covalent bond cannot have ionic character, or that bond classification is all-or-nothing.
probes: Why does the large C-F electronegativity difference distribute the shared electrons unevenly?
How can a bond be covalent by classification yet have significant ionic character?
How does that polarity contribute to the bond's strength?
Where does C-F sit on the ionic-covalent continuum, and why is it not fully ionic?

62.misconception: Not recognizing the lone pair as the source of basicity, or confusing Bronsted and Lewis base behavior.
probes: Why does the nitrogen lone pair make nicotine basic (proton acceptor / electron-pair donor)?
Distinguish a Bronsted base (accepts H+) from a Lewis base (donates a pair).
How does that same lone pair enable binding to a receptor site?
What would reduce this basicity (delocalization of the lone pair)?

63.misconception: Believing a single Lewis structure with distinct single and double bonds is correct, not recognizing delocalization / equal bond lengths.
probes: Why can no single Lewis structure show three equal C-O bonds?
What does the equal bond length tell you about the electron distribution (delocalization)?
How do multiple resonance forms combine into a single hybrid?
How does delocalization stabilize the ion?

64.misconception: Choosing a Lewis structure by gut feel, or misapplying formal charge (e.g. placing positive formal charge on the more electronegative atom).
probes: How do you calculate the formal charge on an atom in a proposed structure?
What makes a structure with large or oddly placed formal charges less reasonable?
Why is positive formal charge on a highly electronegative atom unfavorable?
Use formal charge to compare two candidate structures for SiO4^4-.

65.misconception: Treating the amide nitrogen like an ordinary amine, ignoring lone-pair delocalization into the carbonyl.
probes: Why does the nitrogen lone pair delocalize into the adjacent C=O (conjugation)?
What does the resonance hybrid look like (partial C=N, partial C-O single bond)?
Why does tying up the lone pair make the nitrogen a weaker base than an amine?
How would breaking that conjugation change its basicity?

66.misconception: Attributing the planarity to coincidence rather than to conjugation requiring coplanar p-orbital overlap.
probes: Why does delocalization require the participating atoms to be coplanar (p-orbital overlap)?
Why would twisting the ring break conjugation and raise the energy?
How does that lock the molecule into a planar, rigid shape?
Contrast with a non-conjugated ring that can pucker freely.

67.misconception: Assuming all polymers have the same intermolecular forces, ignoring how C-Cl dipoles add dipole-dipole attraction.
probes: Why is the C-Cl bond polar while C-C and C-H are essentially nonpolar?
How do permanent dipoles create dipole-dipole attractions between PVC chains?
Why are those stronger than the dispersion forces in polyethylene?
How does stronger interchain attraction change rigidity and glass-transition temperature?

68.misconception: Treating every shared pair as a standard covalent bond, not recognizing that both electrons can come from one atom.
probes: In a coordinate/dative bond, where do both shared electrons originate (the donor)?
Why is the Fe-N bond best described this way (nitrogen lone pair into an empty Fe orbital)?
How does this differ from an ordinary covalent bond (one electron from each atom)?
Once formed, is a dative bond distinguishable from a normal covalent bond?

69.misconception: Defaulting to 'covalent' for every bond, or not using the electronegativity difference to classify.
probes: What is the electronegativity difference between iron and oxygen telling you?
Why does a large difference favor electron transfer (ionic) over sharing (covalent)?
How does the resulting cation-anion electrostatic attraction define ionic bonding?
Where is the ionic-covalent boundary fuzzy (percent ionic character)?

70.misconception: Equating polar bonds with a polar molecule, ignoring that symmetric geometry cancels the bond dipoles.
probes: Why is each C-F bond strongly polar (the electronegativity of fluorine)?
What is the molecular geometry of CF4 (tetrahedral), and how are the bond dipoles arranged?
Why do four symmetric bond dipoles cancel to give zero net dipole?
Contrast with a molecule where they do not cancel (e.g. CHF3 or H2O).

71.misconception: Citing 'polarity' vaguely without identifying hydrogen bonding through the two -OH groups.
probes: Why can each -OH group both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water?
How do two -OH groups per molecule strengthen the attraction to water?
Why does this make the molecule hygroscopic (water-attracting)?
Contrast with a similar molecule that has no -OH groups.

72.misconception: Assuming temperature changes the chemistry, rather than helping molecules overcome intermolecular attractions.
probes: What intermolecular forces hold BPA within the polymer (dispersion, dipole-dipole)?
Why does higher temperature help more molecules overcome those forces?
Why does this increase the rate and extent of leaching?
Connect the kinetic-energy distribution to the fraction of molecules able to escape.

73.misconception: Not identifying ion-dipole forces, or thinking the salt chemically reacts with the ice.
probes: What forces form between Na+/Cl- ions and polar water molecules (ion-dipole)?
Why are those strong enough to pull water out of the ordered ice lattice?
How does disrupting the hydrogen-bond network lower the freezing point?
Why does this work even below 0 C?
